description: Decision-making rules for combining image analysis, user preferences, occasion, color, fit, footwear, accessories, grooming, and style knowledge into final fashion recommendations.

rules.rule: Use explicitly provided user information as the highest-confidence input.
Use image-derived information only when the visual evidence is sufficiently clear.
Do not override explicit user preferences with generic fashion rules unless there is a clear practical or occasion conflict.
Use occasion requirements before subjective style preferences when the user specifies a formal dress code.
Use weather information when it materially affects clothing practicality.
Use cultural or venue information when explicitly provided.
Do not invent missing user preferences.
Do not invent missing occasion details.
Do not invent clothing attributes that cannot be reasonably identified from the image.
When reliable user information conflicts with uncertain image interpretation, prefer the user information.
Use structured image analysis as the bridge between the uploaded image and knowledge-base rules.
Identify visible garments before applying styling recommendations.
Identify visible colors before applying color-matching rules.
Identify visible fit or silhouette before applying fit recommendations.
Identify footwear before applying footwear-specific recommendations.
Identify visible accessories before applying accessory recommendations.
Identify visible grooming characteristics only when the image provides sufficient detail.
Separate observed facts from inferred style classifications.
Do not treat an inferred garment type as certain when the image is ambiguous.
Use confidence values for important image-derived attributes.
The recommendation process should follow analysis, context detection, rule retrieval, rule prioritization, recommendation generation, and validation.
Do not generate the final recommendation before identifying the major outfit components.
Determine the primary occasion before judging occasion suitability.
Determine the intended style direction before suggesting style-specific changes.
Retrieve rules relevant to the detected clothing attributes instead of applying every knowledge-base rule.
Prioritize rules that directly relate to the user's request.
Apply high-impact rules before low-impact styling details.
Validate the proposed recommendation against occasion, color, fit, footwear, and practicality.
If the proposed change creates a new major mismatch, reject or modify that change.
The final recommendation should be internally consistent across all visible outfit components.
Select rules using garment type, color, fit, occasion, style, footwear, accessories, grooming, weather, and user preference.
Do not apply rules unrelated to the detected outfit.
Prefer specific rules over broad generic rules when both apply.
Prefer occasion-specific rules over general casual or formal rules.
Prefer explicit dress-code rules over aesthetic style rules.
Prefer practical weather rules when weather creates a direct clothing constraint.
Prefer user-specific preferences when multiple recommendations are otherwise equally suitable.
Avoid stacking multiple rules that produce the same recommendation.
Use the smallest relevant rule set capable of explaining the recommendation.
When no specific rule applies, fall back to general coordination principles.
Prioritize safety and practical suitability over aesthetic preference.
Prioritize explicit dress code over personal experimentation.
Prioritize weather suitability over optional aesthetic details.
Prioritize major fit problems over minor accessory issues.
Prioritize major color clashes over minor styling imperfections.
Prioritize occasion mismatch over personal style experimentation.
Prioritize footwear practicality when the activity requires substantial walking or movement.
Prioritize garment condition when the event is formal or professional.
Prioritize the user's explicit desired outcome when no major constraint is violated.
Do not prioritize a minor aesthetic improvement over a major practical requirement.
When two rules conflict, determine which rule has higher contextual relevance.
Specific occasion rules should generally override broad style rules.
Explicit user constraints should generally override optional style preferences.
Weather constraints should override purely aesthetic layering recommendations.
Cultural requirements should be considered when explicitly relevant to the occasion.
When two valid styles conflict, select the style that better matches the requested occasion.
When evidence is insufficient to resolve a conflict, present the uncertainty instead of inventing certainty.
Do not combine contradictory recommendations into a confusing final outfit.
If two changes have similar value, prefer the less disruptive change.
If a recommendation repeatedly conflicts with reliable user preferences, adapt the recommendation rather than ignoring the preferences.
Do not change an outfit component unless there is a clear reason.
If the outfit is already suitable, recommend keeping the core outfit.
Prefer one high-impact change over several low-impact changes.
Change footwear first when footwear is the primary source of formality mismatch.
Change the outer layer first when layering is the primary source of style mismatch.
Change the bottom when the silhouette or occasion mismatch mainly comes from the lower half.
Change the top when the upper garment conflicts strongly with the occasion.
Use accessories as a final refinement rather than the first solution to a major outfit problem.
Do not recommend replacing multiple garments when one adjustment solves the primary issue.
Preserve items that already satisfy the requested style.
Use the colour-theory knowledge base when evaluating outfit color relationships.
Do not re-evaluate every color combination if an applicable color rule already exists.
Prioritize dominant color relationships before small accessory color details.
Use color contrast when the outfit needs clearer visual separation.
Use tonal coordination when the requested style is minimalist or understated.
Avoid adding another strong accent color when the outfit already contains a dominant statement color.
Consider footwear as part of the overall color balance.
Consider visible accessories as part of the overall color repetition strategy.
Do not reject an outfit solely because it does not follow a generic three-color guideline when the overall combination is coherent.
When color identification is uncertain, use cautious language instead of precise unsupported color names.
Use the fit-and-silhouette knowledge base when evaluating proportions.
Evaluate top and bottom proportions together rather than independently.
Consider silhouette before recommending a new garment solely for trend reasons.
Avoid recommending oversized pieces without evaluating the existing outfit volume.
Avoid recommending slim pieces without considering the intended overall silhouette.
Use consistent silhouette language across the final recommendation.
When the user prefers a specific fit, preserve that preference when occasion permits.
Do not infer exact body measurements from a single image.
Do not make body-shape claims when image evidence is insufficient.
Use garment proportions rather than unsupported body measurements when explaining fit recommendations.
Use the footwear-and-accessories knowledge base when evaluating footwear or accessories.
Evaluate footwear based on occasion, outfit style, color, and practicality.
Do not recommend footwear solely because it is fashionable if it conflicts with the occasion.
Use clean minimal footwear when the intended style is understated.
Use refined footwear when the outfit needs a formality upgrade.
Use practical footwear when weather or activity requires it.
Avoid unnecessary footwear changes when the current footwear already suits the occasion.
Evaluate footwear and trousers together when judging the lower-body visual balance.
Consider footwear condition when recommending outfits for formal or professional settings.
If footwear is not visible, do not invent its style or color.
Accessories should support the primary outfit direction.
Use accessories to refine an already coherent outfit rather than rescue a major mismatch.
Avoid recommending several statement accessories simultaneously.
Match accessory formality to the occasion.
Use restrained accessories for formal and professional contexts.
More expressive accessories can be considered for casual, streetwear, party, or content contexts.
Use accessory color repetition when it improves visual cohesion.
Do not force color repetition when it makes the outfit visually crowded.
Consider practical accessories when the activity requires them.
If an accessory is unclear in the image, describe it cautiously or omit it from the recommendation.
Use the grooming knowledge base when hairstyle, beard, sunglasses, or grooming coordination is requested.
Do not force grooming recommendations into an outfit request when grooming is irrelevant.
Coordinate grooming formality with the occasion.
Use subtle grooming refinements for professional settings.
More expressive grooming can be considered for casual or fashion-content contexts.
Do not make sensitive or unsupported assumptions about facial characteristics.
Do not infer exact face shape when the image angle prevents reliable analysis.
If sunglasses are already suitable, do not recommend changing them without a specific reason.
Grooming recommendations should complement rather than dominate outfit recommendations.
Separate outfit recommendations from optional grooming recommendations in the final output.
Use the occasion-and-style knowledge base as the primary source for occasion suitability.
Identify whether the occasion is casual, smart casual, professional, formal, festive, social, active, or another relevant category.
Use venue context when it materially changes the appropriate formality.
Use time of day as a supporting factor rather than the sole decision factor.
Use cultural context when explicitly provided.
Use weather context when relevant to clothing practicality.
If occasion information is missing, classify cautiously using visible clothing and context.
Do not declare an outfit inappropriate when the occasion itself is unknown.
When multiple occasions are plausible, recommend the most flexible reasonable styling direction.
Clearly distinguish occasion suitability from personal fashion preference.
Identify the dominant style direction before adding style-specific recommendations.
Possible style directions include casual, smart casual, classic, minimalist, streetwear, festive, formal, and premium-inspired.
Do not label an outfit with multiple conflicting aesthetics unless the combination is intentional.
Preserve the dominant visual direction when making small improvements.
Use personal style preferences to select between equally suitable alternatives.
Do not force a trend into an outfit if it weakens the intended style.
Use trend elements selectively when the user explicitly wants a trend-focused look.
Keep minimalist recommendations visually restrained.
Keep streetwear recommendations proportionally intentional.
Keep classic recommendations focused on versatile and coherent pieces.
Ask or use explicit preferences for color, fit, style, budget, comfort, and occasion when available.
Do not assume the user wants a particular fashion aesthetic.
If the user dislikes an item type, avoid recommending it unless required by the occasion.
If the user prefers oversized clothing, preserve oversized styling where the occasion permits.
If the user prefers minimal styling, reduce unnecessary accessories and visual complexity.
If the user prefers streetwear, use streetwear-compatible alternatives when occasion allows.
If the user prefers classic clothing, prioritize timeless alternatives when they meet the occasion.
If the user prioritizes comfort, avoid recommending unnecessary restrictive garments.
If budget is provided, do not recommend options that clearly violate the stated budget.
User preference should influence the recommendation without overriding major practical requirements.
When the user provides available wardrobe items, prioritize those items before suggesting new purchases.
Use existing wardrobe pieces whenever they can satisfy the requested occasion.
Do not recommend buying a new item when an existing item can solve the same styling problem.
When multiple wardrobe items are suitable, prefer combinations with stronger coordination and versatility.
Use wardrobe availability as a hard constraint only when the user asks for outfit combinations from existing clothes.
When a required garment is unavailable, suggest the closest available alternative.
Do not assume the user owns a specific garment unless it is provided or stored as wardrobe data.
Prefer versatile wardrobe combinations that can work across multiple occasions.
Consider repeated use when generating wardrobe recommendations.
When recommending a purchase, clearly distinguish it from items already available in the wardrobe.
Classify recommendations as essential, recommended, optional, or preference-based.
Essential changes should address clear occasion, practicality, or major coordination problems.
Recommended changes should provide a meaningful improvement but are not mandatory.
Optional changes should be presented as style refinements.
Preference-based suggestions should depend on the user's known style choices.
Do not present optional style preferences as objective requirements.
Do not use strong language when evidence is weak.
Use stronger recommendation language when multiple independent rules support the same change.
Use weaker recommendation language when the change depends on subjective preference.
Do not create a problem merely to provide a recommendation.
Evaluate outfit suitability using multiple dimensions rather than a single score.
Relevant dimensions include occasion fit, color coordination, silhouette, footwear, accessories, practicality, and style coherence.
Do not allow a strong score in one dimension to completely hide a major failure in another dimension.
Major occasion mismatch should significantly reduce overall suitability.
Major weather or activity mismatch should significantly reduce practical suitability.
Minor accessory imperfections should have lower impact than major fit or occasion issues.
An already coherent outfit should not receive a low suitability assessment because it lacks optional trend elements.
A recommendation score should represent contextual suitability rather than objective attractiveness.
Do not expose an internal score unless the product UI explicitly requires it.
Use scores internally to prioritize recommendations, not as a substitute for explanation.
Calculate confidence separately for image recognition and recommendation suitability.
High-confidence image attributes can support stronger recommendations.
Low-confidence image attributes should not be the sole basis for major changes.
Confidence should decrease when garments are partially hidden.
Confidence should decrease when image quality prevents reliable color or texture identification.
Confidence should decrease when the image angle prevents reliable fit interpretation.
Confidence should decrease when the occasion is inferred without contextual information.
Do not convert low-confidence visual observations into definitive statements.
If critical information is uncertain, provide a conditional recommendation.
The final recommendation should reflect uncertainty without becoming unnecessarily vague.
Every meaningful recommendation should have a clear reason.
Explain recommendations using observable outfit characteristics whenever possible.
Explain color changes using color relationships rather than vague statements.
Explain fit changes using silhouette and proportion.
Explain footwear changes using formality, color, style, or practicality.
Explain accessory changes using visual balance or occasion suitability.
Explain grooming changes using occasion or coordination rather than unsupported appearance judgments.
Avoid generic explanations such as 'this looks better' without identifying why.
Keep explanations concise enough for a consumer-facing styling interface.
If the user asks why a recommendation was made, expose the relevant reasoning factors in simple language.
Provide alternatives only when they meaningfully differ.
Avoid generating many nearly identical outfit alternatives.
When giving alternatives, change one or two major dimensions at a time.
Useful alternative dimensions include footwear, layering, color, silhouette, and formality.
Alternative one should generally preserve the user's original outfit where possible.
Alternative recommendations should remain consistent with the requested occasion.
Do not present an alternative that violates an explicit user constraint.
If one recommendation is clearly sufficient, do not add alternatives unnecessarily.
Use alternatives to express style preference rather than uncertainty when the base recommendation is already reliable.
Clearly label alternatives by their purpose, such as more casual, more formal, or more expressive.
Do not recommend a garment solely because it is currently trending.
Do not recommend a color solely because it is popular.
Do not recommend accessories solely to make the response longer.
Do not claim that an outfit is objectively attractive.
Do not make unsupported claims about body shape.
Do not infer income, social status, personality, or lifestyle from clothing.
Do not claim an item is expensive or cheap unless price information is available.
Do not claim that a recommendation guarantees a particular social outcome.
Do not invent brands, products, prices, or availability.
Do not describe uncertain image details as confirmed facts.
If the uploaded outfit is already coherent, identify what is working before suggesting improvements.
Do not assume every uploaded outfit needs correction.
Preserve successful color relationships when making other changes.
Preserve successful silhouette relationships when changing colors or accessories.
Preserve appropriate footwear unless it creates a specific mismatch.
Preserve the user's favorite garment when reasonable.
When improving an outfit, identify the highest-impact weakness first.
If there are no major weaknesses, focus on optional refinements.
Do not create contradictory changes that remove an outfit's original visual identity.
Use the uploaded outfit as the baseline for adaptation unless the user requests a completely new look.
When adapting the same outfit to another occasion, preserve compatible garments whenever possible.
Use footwear changes to move between casual and more refined occasions when appropriate.
Use outer layers to increase or decrease perceived formality.
Use accessories to refine the outfit after the major occasion requirements are satisfied.
Do not force a casual outfit into a formal setting if the core garments cannot reasonably support the dress code.
Do not make an outfit unnecessarily formal when adapting it to a casual setting.
For day-to-night adaptation, change only the elements necessary for the venue and activity.
For summer-to-winter adaptation, add practical layers while maintaining the original color direction.
For casual-to-office adaptation, prioritize refined footwear, structured garments, and cleaner finishing.
For office-to-evening adaptation, use one or two deliberate changes rather than rebuilding the outfit.
Combine occasion and weather before selecting the final outfit.
Combine occasion and silhouette before recommending major fit changes.
Combine occasion and footwear before deciding footwear suitability.
Combine style and color before adding statement accessories.
Combine grooming and occasion when grooming recommendations are requested.
Combine user preference and occasion when selecting between multiple valid styles.
Combine activity and footwear when practical movement is important.
Combine time of day and weather when choosing layering.
Combine venue and dress code when both are available.
Do not evaluate any single outfit component completely independently from the rest of the outfit.
Before returning a recommendation, verify that all suggested garments can logically be worn together.
Verify that the recommended outfit matches the requested occasion.
Verify that the color relationships remain coherent after suggested changes.
Verify that the silhouette remains intentional after suggested changes.
Verify that footwear remains appropriate after changing the outfit.
Verify that accessories do not create unnecessary visual clutter.
Verify that weather requirements are respected when weather information is available.
Verify that explicit user constraints are not violated.
Verify that no unsupported factual claims are included.
Reject the recommendation if it creates a larger problem than the issue it was intended to solve.
The final recommendation should clearly state the primary outfit direction.
The final recommendation should identify the most important suggested change.
The final recommendation should include a short reason for the main suggestion.
Include secondary suggestions only when they provide meaningful additional value.
Separate optional suggestions from essential recommendations.
Use simple consumer-friendly language.
Avoid excessive technical fashion terminology unless the user requests detailed styling knowledge.
Avoid repeating the same recommendation in multiple sections.
When uncertainty matters, clearly mention the uncertain element.
The final response should be concise enough for a mobile AI stylist interface.
The recommendation engine should produce structured fields before generating natural-language output.
Structured output should contain detected outfit components.
Structured output should contain the detected or requested occasion.
Structured output should contain the dominant style direction.
Structured output should contain key strengths of the outfit.
Structured output should contain key issues only when meaningful issues exist.
Structured output should contain recommended changes.
Structured output should contain confidence information when image interpretation is uncertain.
Structured output should distinguish observed attributes from recommended attributes.
Natural-language output should be generated from validated structured recommendation data.
Do not generate a recommendation merely because a knowledge-base rule exists.
Use multiple supporting signals when recommending a major outfit change.
Avoid recommendations based on a single weak visual observation.
Check for contradictions between color, fit, occasion, and style recommendations.
Check that recommended garments are compatible with the user's stated preferences.
Check that the recommendation does not unnecessarily replace successful outfit elements.
Check that optional suggestions are clearly presented as optional.
Check that uncertainty is reflected in the final confidence level.
Check that the final explanation matches the actual rules used.
Do not claim that the recommendation was based on information that was not actually available.
If the outfit is already suitable, return a keep-and-refine recommendation rather than a complete replacement.
If the outfit has one major issue, focus the recommendation on that issue.
If the outfit has multiple major issues, prioritize them by occasion impact, practicality, fit, color, and refinement.
If the outfit cannot satisfy the requested occasion without major changes, clearly state that the current combination needs substantial adaptation.
If required information is missing, use a flexible recommendation rather than inventing details.
If user asks for a quick recommendation, prioritize the highest-impact answer and omit secondary explanations.
If user asks for detailed reasoning, expose the major factors and rule interactions.
If user requests multiple outfit options, generate clearly differentiated options that satisfy the same core requirements.
If user requests only a rating, use contextual suitability criteria and avoid presenting subjective taste as objective fact.
The recommendation engine should always prefer coherent, explainable, context-aware recommendations over generic fashion advice.
